Sparse and dense retrieval are complementary on web-scale corpora

M. Okafor, L. Bergstrom, S. Haddad
Abstract. We study sparse lexical retrieval and dense embedding retrieval on a corpus of 1.2 billion web pages. Neither retriever dominates: BM25 wins on queries containing rare identifiers and quoted phrases, while a dense bi-encoder wins on paraphrased and multi-hop questions. We propose a fusion rule that combines the two scores after per-query normalisation, and we show a 6.4 point nDCG improvement over the best single retriever.

We evaluate on three query sets and report latency, memory and dollar cost per thousand queries. The sparse retriever serves a query in four milliseconds from an inverted index held in RAM; the dense retriever needs a GPU to stay under fifty milliseconds.

Our conclusion is that a production search system should keep both retrievers and route between them, rather than choosing one. The routing signal is the query itself: identifier-heavy queries go sparse, natural language questions go dense.
